plan.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound) vs Semaglutide (Wegovy): Who Lost More in the Obesity Head-to-Head Trial?' (adults without diabetes are stated in the first spoken line). Hook: 'In Sept 2026 Lilly reported an indirect comparison against Wegovy HD. But one trial in adults with obesity and no diabetes actually randomized people to the two drugs.' Section 2 adds one line: 'An earlier trial, SURPASS-2, compared them in type 2 diabetes at lower semaglutide doses. That's a different population.' Everything else as planned. Every SURMOUNT-5 number carries the treatment-regimen estimand, 72 wk, arm (maximum tolerated dose) and comparator. Wegovy HD gets one line: 'FDA-approved Mar 19 2026, studied in STEP UP, a separate trial, not head-to-head.' Close with the prescriber line.

plan.why: Fits our proven long-form format (named drugs, 'X vs Y: which', tirzepatide in the title) and rests on a peer-reviewed RCT that will pass the fact-check. Search demand for Zepbound vs Wegovy is rising. | fact-check: Verified: SURMOUNT-5 (Aronne et al., NEJM, May 11 2025). 751 randomized, open-label, Lilly-sponsored, maximum tolerated dose (tirzepatide 10 or 15 mg vs semaglutide 1.7 or 2.4 mg, weekly). LS-mean weight change at 72 wk was −20.2% vs −13.7% (about 22.8 kg vs 15.0 kg). Population: adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Wegovy HD (semaglutide 7.2 mg) was FDA-approved Mar 19 2026. Lilly's indirect comparison (SURMOUNT-1 vs STEP UP) was a press release on Sep 29 2026, presented at EASD 2026. MAJOR scope error: 'the only randomized head-to-head trial so far' is false. SURPASS-2 (NEJM 2021) randomized tirzepatide against semaglutide 1 mg in type 2 diabetes. It must read 'the only head-to-head trial in people with obesity WITHOUT diabetes' (or 'the obesity head-to-head'). Other fixes: (a) drop 'just released' from the hook. The press release is 2+ weeks old and news fades. Use 'In Sept 2026, Lilly reported an indirect comparison…', label it as a company press release, and give its estimand. (b) The doses in the trial arms are fine as arm labels. Never present 7.2 mg eligibility or step-up rules (the label's 'after tolerating 2.4 mg for 4 weeks') as instructions. (c) Copy waist change, ≥15%/≥25% shares, GI AEs and AE-related discontinuation per arm exactly from the NEJM paper, with the treatment-regimen estimand stated. (d) Keep 'Lilly-sponsored' in every caption. (e) The title must name the population. Include the 'not right for everyone' and 'don't stop or switch on your own' lines.

package.description:
Tirzepatide vs semaglutide: SURMOUNT-5 (NEJM, 2025) is the only randomized head-to-head obesity trial so far. 751 adults with obesity and no diabetes were assigned to either drug at the maximum tolerated dose for 72 weeks.
Main analysis, average weight loss: 20.2% with tirzepatide vs 13.7% with semaglutide, a 6.5-point gap. Side effects were mostly gut-related in both groups. Open-label, Lilly-sponsored.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. These are prescription medicines, and they aren't right for everyone — talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether either one is right for you, and don't stop, start or switch on your own.

Sources:
1. Aronne LJ et al., SURMOUNT-5, NEJM, 2025: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2416394
2. Eli Lilly, indirect comparison press release, Sept 29, 2026: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/lillys-zepbound-tirzepatide-10-mg-and-15-mg-was-associated-with-more-weight-loss-than-wegovy-hd-semaglutide-injection-7-2-mg-in-a-new-indirect-treatment-comparison-302892601.html
3. Novo Nordisk, Wegovy HD FDA approval press release, Mar 19, 2026: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/fda-approves-novo-nordisks-new-wegovy-hd-injection-delivering-the-highest-weight-loss-to-date-for-a-wegovy-injection-adding-to-its-already-expansive-clinical-profile-302718982.html

Both worked, and the groups overlapped a lot. Side effects were mostly gut-related in both groups, mainly while doses were being raised. Save this for your next appointment. script.working_title: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) vs Semaglutide (Wegovy): Who Lost More in the Obesity Head-to-Head Trial?
script.hook_pattern: Stakes + specificity, answer first. The first line names the population (adults with obesity and no diabetes) and says only one randomized trial has compared the two drugs in that group. The result (20.2% vs 13.7%) arrives within about 15 seconds. An open loop follows ('the one result that tells you more than the winner') and pays off in 'The result that matters most'.

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide or semaglutide? In adults with obesity and no diabetes, only one randomized trial so far has put these two weekly shots head-to-head.
scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: the viewer's exact question, with the population named in the first line

scenes.narration: You may have seen a Lilly press release from September 2026 reporting that tirzepatide 10 and 15 milligrams was linked to more weight loss than high-dose Wegovy. That was an indirect comparison, built from two separate trials, SURMOUNT-1 and STEP UP.

visual.stock_query: two separate race tracks side by side

scenes.retention_device: Contrast setup: indirect comparison vs a truly randomized trial

scenes.narration: SURMOUNT-5 is different. It randomly assigned 751 adults to one drug or the other, and followed them for 72 weeks.

visual.stock_query: crowd of cartoon adults split two groups

scenes.narration: So, who lost more? At 72 weeks, in the main treatment-regimen analysis, people assigned to tirzepatide lost an average of 20.2% of their body weight, versus 13.7% with semaglutide, each at the maximum tolerated dose.
scenes.retention_device: Answers the title's question within 15 seconds

scenes.narration: But that headline hides something. By the end of this video, you'll see the one result that tells you more than the winner does, and why it changes the question you take to your doctor.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop (paid off in 'The result that matters most')

scenes.narration: First: why does one randomized trial beat a pile of comparisons across studies?
Picture two runners who raced on different days, on different tracks, in different weather. You'd learn something. But you wouldn't know who's faster.
Cross-trial comparisons have the same problem. Different people, different placebo groups, even different lengths.
Semaglutide's big obesity trial, STEP 1, ran 68 weeks. Tirzepatide's, SURMOUNT-1, ran 72. Even the clocks don't match.
Randomization fixes that. Chance, not choice, decides who gets which drug, so the two groups start out alike and face the same conditions.
An earlier trial, SURPASS-2, compared them in type 2 diabetes at lower semaglutide doses. That's a different population.

visual.fact: SURPASS-2 compared them in type 2 diabetes

scenes.narration: And the newer high-dose semaglutide, Wegovy HD? The FDA approved it on March 19, 2026, based on STEP UP, a separate trial, not head-to-head against tirzepatide.
So for adults with obesity and no diabetes, SURMOUNT-5 is the cleanest comparison we have. But who exactly signed up?
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before the section change

scenes.narration: Let's meet the people in the trial, because the results apply most clearly to people like them.
Participants had a BMI of 30 or more, or a BMI of 27 or more with at least one weight-related condition, such as high blood pressure or sleep apnea.

items: Or BMI 27+ with a weight-related condition
e.g. high blood pressure, sleep apnea

scenes.narration: None had diabetes. So these results don't automatically carry over to people who do.
Their average starting weight was about 113 kilograms, roughly 250 pounds. And the trial ran at sites across the United States and Puerto Rico.

visual.stock_query: map of US and Puerto Rico

scenes.narration: Everyone got one injection a week. Doses were raised in steps to each person's maximum tolerated dose: 10 or 15 milligrams of tirzepatide, or 1.7 or 2.4 milligrams of semaglutide.
Those are trial arms, not a recipe. Your prescriber decides your dose.
Two more details. The trial was open-label, so everyone knew which drug they were on. And it was sponsored by Lilly, the company that makes tirzepatide.
Neither detail makes the result wrong. But keep them in your back pocket. They'll matter later.
scenes.retention_device: Mini open loop (paid off in 'What it can't tell you')

scenes.narration: Now the main result. But first, one piece of jargon that changes how you read every number: the estimand.
The main analysis used the treatment-regimen estimand. In plain English, it counts everyone who was randomized, including people who stopped their drug along the way.
That's a stricter test. It doesn't just count the people who stuck with it perfectly.
Using that estimand, at 72 weeks, people on tirzepatide at the maximum tolerated dose lost an average of 20.2% of their body weight.
People on semaglutide at the maximum tolerated dose lost an average of 13.7% over the same 72 weeks.
That's a gap of 6.5 percentage points in tirzepatide's favor, a statistically significant difference.
In kilograms, same estimand, same 72 weeks: about 22.8 for tirzepatide versus 15.0 for semaglutide. That's roughly 50 pounds versus 33.

Here's what people miss: 13.7% is a big number. In semaglutide's own trial, STEP 1, also in adults without diabetes, the placebo group lost 2.4% over 68 weeks, versus 14.9% on semaglutide 2.4 milligrams.

visual.myth: Semaglutide 'lost' this trial, so it barely works

scenes.narration: So this isn't a story about one drug working and one failing. Both worked. One worked more, on average.
And 'on average' is doing a lot of work. Think of a city's average temperature: true, but not what you'll feel on your day.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook that sets up the next section

scenes.narration: So let's look past the average.
Waist size first. Treatment-regimen estimand, 72 weeks: waists shrank by 18.4 centimeters on tirzepatide versus 13.0 on semaglutide. That's about 7 inches versus 5.
Now milestones. At 72 weeks, 64.6% of the tirzepatide group reached at least 15% weight loss, versus 40.1% of the semaglutide group.
At least 25%, a full quarter of body weight: 31.6% on tirzepatide, versus 16.1% on semaglutide. Roughly 1 in 3, versus 1 in 6.

visual.stock_query: one in three vs one in six icons

scenes.narration: The same rules apply to all of these: treatment-regimen estimand, each drug at its maximum tolerated dose, at 72 weeks.
Hold on to that 1 in 6. It's half of the surprise I promised. But first, the question everyone asks: what about side effects?

visual.stock_query: sticky note reading one in six

scenes.retention_device: Partial payoff that opens the side-effects question

scenes.narration: Here's how the two compared on side effects.

visual.stock_query: two stomachs side by side calm

scenes.narration: In both groups, the most common side effects were gastrointestinal. Think nausea, diarrhea, constipation and vomiting, which both drug labels list as common.
Most were mild to moderate, and they showed up mainly while doses were being stepped up.
Over the trial, 6.1% of the tirzepatide group stopped treatment because of side effects, versus 8.0% of the semaglutide group.
That's a small gap, in an open-label trial. Read it as a hint, not a verdict on which drug is gentler.
If you're on either one, habits that may help with nausea include smaller meals, eating slowly, and stopping when you feel comfortably full.
For constipation, fluids and fibre can help, unless you've been told to limit fluids. And if side effects are rough, tell your prescriber instead of adjusting anything yourself.
Now, remember those back-pocket details? Here's where they come in.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to the earlier loop that opens the next section

scenes.narration: Every trial has edges. Here are five things SURMOUNT-5 can't tell you.
One: it doesn't explain why tirzepatide lost more. Tirzepatide acts on two hormone receptors, GIP and GLP-1. Semaglutide acts on GLP-1. But the trial wasn't built to prove that's the reason.

visual.stock_query: two keys versus one key lock

scenes.retention_device: Pushes back on an easy assumption

scenes.narration: Two: it was open-label. Everyone knew their drug, and a blinded trial would have removed that variable.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the first back-pocket detail

scenes.narration: Three: semaglutide went up to 2.4 milligrams, not the newer 7.2. So it can't tell you how tirzepatide stacks up against Wegovy HD.
Four: no one had diabetes. For type 2 diabetes, SURPASS-2 is the head-to-head, with different doses and a different population.
Five: it stopped at 72 weeks. It can't show what happens over five or ten years, or after someone stops.
On that last point, another trial gives a clue. In SURMOUNT-4, adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, and no diabetes, took tirzepatide for 36 weeks.
Then some were switched to placebo. From week 36 to week 88, their weight went back up by 14.0% on average, while those who stayed on tirzepatide lost another 5.5%.

visual.stat_label: Avg weight change from week 36 to 88

scenes.narration: That's not advice to stay on or come off anything. It's a reason to make that decision with your prescriber. Don't stop or switch on your own.
So here's the result I promised, the one that tells you more than the winner. It's the overlap between the two groups.
Remember, 16.1% of the semaglutide group lost at least a quarter of their body weight.
Meanwhile, about 35% of the tirzepatide group didn't reach 15%. So a good chunk of people on semaglutide lost more than a good chunk on tirzepatide.
And nearly 1 in 5 people on tirzepatide didn't reach even 10%.
All of these were counted the same strict way, at 72 weeks. So the average tells you which drug tends to do more. It can't tell you how your body will respond.
That's why the winner on average isn't automatically the right pick for you. Side effects, your health history, other conditions, cost and coverage, and your preferences all count.
These medicines also aren't right for everyone. Both labels say not to use them if you or a family member have had medullary thyroid cancer, or if you have a condition called MEN 2.
And remember the sponsor. Lilly funded SURMOUNT-5. It's peer-reviewed, in the New England Journal of Medicine, but the funder is always worth knowing.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the second back-pocket detail

scenes.narration: Whichever drug you end up on, here's how to get the most from it.
Both are approved alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. The shot is one part of the plan, not the whole plan.
Protein at every meal is a common recommendation to help protect muscle while you lose weight. If you have kidney disease, check with your clinician first.
Strength training matters too. Guidelines recommend muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days a week. Start gently, with bands or bodyweight moves, and build up.
Sip fluids through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids. And slow down at meals. These medicines can make you feel full sooner, so give that signal time to land.
And keep perspective. Weight is one health measure among many. Energy, blood pressure, sleep and strength count too.
Let's wrap it into a checklist you can actually use.
One: in adults with obesity and no diabetes, tirzepatide at the maximum tolerated dose led to more weight loss on average than semaglutide, 20.2% versus 13.7% at 72 weeks, in the main analysis.
Two: semaglutide still produced large losses, and the groups overlapped a lot.
Three: side effects were mostly gastrointestinal in both groups, and mostly during dose increases.
Four: the trial didn't test high-dose semaglutide, people with diabetes, or life beyond 72 weeks.
Questions for your doctor: Which option fits my health history? How will we handle side effects? And how will we protect my muscle?

factcheck.summary: I checked every number and source claim that matters, and the script is accurate. SURMOUNT-5 (NEJM 2025, Lilly-sponsored, open-label) checks out on every count: 751 adults, sites in the US and Puerto Rico, maximum tolerated doses of 10/15 mg tirzepatide vs 1.7/2.4 mg semaglutide, and 72 weeks. Under the treatment-regimen estimand the results match: 20.2% vs 13.7% weight lost (a 6.5-point difference), 22.8 vs 15.0 kg, and waist 18.4 vs 13.0 cm. The share reaching each weight-loss milestone also matches: at least 15% (64.6% vs 40.1%) and at least 25% (31.6% vs 16.1%). For at least 10% it was 81.6% vs 60.5%, so the script's "nearly 1 in 5 under 10%" (18.4%) and "about 35% under 15%" are correct. Stopping treatment because of side effects was 6.1% vs 8.0%, and side effects were mostly mild to moderate and mostly during dose increases. The Lilly indirect-comparison press release is dated Sept 29, 2026 and does use SURMOUNT-1 and STEP UP. Wegovy HD (7.2 mg) was FDA-approved on March 19, 2026 based on STEP UP. The SURMOUNT-4 figures (+14.0% vs −5.5%, weeks 36–88) and population, STEP 1 (14.9% vs 2.4%, 68 weeks), the SURPASS-2 scope and the WHO guidance on muscle-strengthening 2+ days a week are all correct. The safety beats are in place: the prescriber line, don't stop or switch on your own, the fluids caveat, the kidney caveat on protein, start gently, the medullary thyroid cancer/MEN 2 warning, the sponsor disclosure and the open-label limitation. The title, hook and open loop all pay off. There are only two small wording fixes. The press-release figures in the transcript came from my fetch tool's summaries, and the NEJM SURMOUNT-5 page wasn't fetched directly, so the SURMOUNT-5 figures were cross-checked against ACC and press coverage (all matched). The baseline weight (~113 kg) wasn't independently confirmed, and the 18.4 vs 13.0 cm waist result was confirmed against an ACC summary that doesn't name the estimand. One outlet gave −20.0 vs −14.7 cm, probably under the other (efficacy) estimand, so keep the script's figures labelled as treatment-regimen.

audio.soundNotes: Music sits right in the -12 to -15 dB window under voice and about the same in pauses, so it reads as present but never competing — no gain change needed. Cue work focused on taming a handful of cues that measured far louder than the -14 to -20 dB during-speech target (notably i167, i325, i489, i493 which were sitting at -5 to -11 dB, nearly as loud as the narrator) and trimming several more modest over-the-target blips/pops (i89, i111, i239, i376, i382, i432, i508, i509, i578, i586, i621, i640) rather than touching the many cues that already land correctly in-range. Dropped two redundant triple-bubble layers (i211, i499) where 4-5 effects were stacking in under a third of a second. Added five bespoke story-beat stings for moments the stock kit can't cover: a clean brand chime on open, a bright 'clean comparison' sting at the headline reveal, a satisfying number-lock tick under the -20.2%/-13.7% stat pair, a low curious drone for 'what it can't tell you,' and a soft, slowed heartbeat-adjacent tone under 'not right for everyone' to let that safety moment breathe without any competing pops.

issues: Red X on Wegovy / green check on Zepbound editorializes a 'winner' before the viewer even watches, which risks feeling misleading since it's a weight-loss magnitude difference, not a pass/fail result — clashes with brand's positive, non-biased tone
Drug names in small pill tags could be tiny at phone size
Red arrow top-right has no clear referent/label, slightly decorative-only but not harmful
Doesn't let viewer guess which number belongs to which drug, which is fine for curiosity but the sub-text 'AVG LOSS, 72 WEEKS' is fairly small
